problem: Geometric SLAM+planner navigation cannot model dynamic actors or semantic/affordance constraints (monsters, lava, low obstacles), while end-to-end RL captures them but is sample-inefficient, generalizes poorly and is uninterpretable.
motivation: Real agents must avoid moving obstacles and respect agent-specific affordances that geometry alone does not encode. Most simulators are static, so the authors use VizDoom with dynamic hazards. Dense per-pixel labels from back-projected interaction outcomes give far richer supervision than sparse RL rewards.
key_idea: Learn a per-pixel navigability (affordance) map via self-supervised, back-projected interaction feedback (e.g. damage), fuse it with a depth-based geometric map, and plan over it with classical A*, using active trajectory sampling to improve sample efficiency.
insight: Learning only the spatial representation and leaving planning classical gives large sample-efficiency and performance gains over end-to-end PPO. In hazard-dense maps affordance-augmented frontier exploration beats geometric frontier by ~60%, and ~10k samples suffice to learn dynamic hazards, whereas RL trained on 20x more samples still does not beat it. Active sampling (entropy-seeking trajectories) beats random sampling with only 40% of the data and by >10% at 100k samples, because rare hazards get sampled. Dynamic behaviour emerges implicitly as larger safety margins, since labels back-projected from past frames encode where actors later appear.
method: Self-supervised labeling: agent walks toward random nearby points; traversed locations are labeled navigable, and locations of damage/bump/stuck are labeled non-navigable; these world locations are back-projected into earlier RGB frames as partial dense labels with unknown pixels masked
Navigability module: ResNet-18 UNet segmentation trained with masked binary cross-entropy (only labeled pixels), pixel weights by inverse distance to the labeled world point

Active trajectory sampling: seed model trained on n random samples; cost map inversely proportional to predictive entropy; agent plans paths through uncertain areas to maximize label entropy; retrain on all data and iterate (20k random + 4x20k active = 100k)

Map construction and fusion: center-scanline depth gives geometric obstacle map; affordance prediction projected to 2D via camera intrinsics; obstacle cells impassable, free cells costed inversely to navigability confidence; egocentric map updates a global allocentric map using noisy odometry

Planning: classical A* on the global cost map with frequent re-planning (every 10 steps), treating dynamic hazards as static obstacles; applied to frontier-based exploration and goal-directed navigation

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 UNet navigability module (trained from scratch on self-supervised data) + classical A* / frontier planner
setting.training_data: ~100k self-supervised samples collected across 60 procedurally generated VizDoom (Oblige) training maps; ablations 5k-100k
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + noisy depth (60° FOV) + scalar damage feedback sensor (training) + noisy odometry (~2% error)
setting.action_space: three macro-actions: move forward, turn left, turn right
setting.privileged: none (damage feedback sensor used for training labels only; navigation goal given in relative coordinates)

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (Fig. 4 exploration area curves, Fig. 5 success vs damage) and text percentages; no numeric tables. Benchmark is custom VizDoom, not a canonical one.
results: In hazard-dense VizDoom maps, affordance-augmented frontier exploration improves area explored by ~60% over geometric frontier and beats PPO-based RL (Chen et al. 2019) by ~70% per the introduction; in hazard-sparse maps it is roughly equal to frontier. For goal-directed navigation, success improves ~45% with the 100k-sample model (25% with one-fifth the data), and active sampling gives >10% more at 100k; humans still explore ~3x more area.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulated VizDoom with a simple 2.5D world; no real-robot experiments, and trial-and-error data collection could be hazardous in the real world
Dynamics of moving obstacles are captured only implicitly from single frames (no spatio-temporal inputs or explicit tracking); a large gap to human performance remains
Requires a feedback sensor (damage, bump) during training, and gains vanish in hazard-sparse environments
builds_on: Learning exploration policies for navigation (Chen et al. 2019)
compares_to: PPO RL navigation with human waypoints
